for_client: Payroll software: 'Nine of the ten salons on this street already pay staff from their phone. You still use the envelope.' (only if true)
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016

opening: Loss letter: the time you are wasting by filing on paper
seller: City of Denver — online tax filing
beat: 'Go Green' letter (1.7%)
measured_by: BIT/Denver randomised trial, N = 32,866
family: time you are losing now
why: The reader's own lost time beat the good of the planet.
for_client: Bookkeeper: 'You lost about five hours last month typing receipts.'
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016

opening: You have been selected for a FREE doctor’s appt.
seller: City of New Orleans — free check-up, text message
beat: 'Txt YES to be contacted to set up a FREE doctor’s appt' alone (1.0%); 'Take care of yourself so you can care for the ones you love' (0.7%)
result: 1.4% replied YES vs 1.0% simple vs 0.7% family line; won again in a second text to those who had not answered
measured_by: BIT/New Orleans randomised trial, N = 21,442
family: you have been selected
why: A true selection of this reader beat the plain offer and the duty to the family.
for_client: Physio: 'You've been picked for one of our 20 free back checks. Text YES and we ring you.' (only when a real list was drawn)
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016

opening: We have reserved a place for you at the CPF Retirement Planning Service in <the following month>
beat: old letter (13.9%); simplified personal letter (19.1%); with infographic (19.9%)
result: 31.1% attended vs 13.9% old letter (+17 points, 2.2x)
measured_by: BIT/MOM randomised trial, N = 1,213
family: a place is already reserved for you
why: It is already his; not going now means giving something up.
for_client: Dentist: 'We have reserved Tuesday 14 March, 9.20, for your check-up. Ring us if another time suits you better.'
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016

opening: 96% of Medway council tax is paid promptly. You are currently in the very small minority of people who have not paid on time.
beat: standard reminder letter (57.3%); letter with a diagram of the collection steps (64.6%)
result: 68.3% paid vs 57.3% standard (+11.0 points)
measured_by: BIT randomised trial, N = 9,134
family: almost everyone here did; you are the few
why: An exact local number, then the reader put outside it.
for_client: Building manager: '96 of 100 flats have signed for the new lift. Yours is one of the four we are waiting for.'
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016

opening: the majority of drivers who receive a parking fine in Louisville pay it within 13 days
beat: no third letter (standard practice)
result: 18.6% paid vs 8.1% without the letter; each letter returned $4.53 net
measured_by: BIT randomised trial, N = 1,831
family: what most people here do, with a number of days
why: It gives the ordinary time in which people like him act.
for_client: Vet: 'Most owners in Elm Road book the booster within 13 days of this card.' (if true)
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016
doubt: Tested against no letter, not against another wording

opening: Courtesy letter: until now we treated your unpaid bill as an oversight; from now on we will consider it a deliberate choice — with a red ‘Pay Now’ stamp
picture: red PAY NOW stamp on the sheet
beat: the bill without the letter
result: raised payment by the due date (report: +13% people paying); $117,000 more net revenue in one monthly cycle if sent to all
measured_by: BIT randomised trial; N in chart
family: silence is now a choice
why: The excuse of forgetting is politely taken away and one action is stamped.
for_client: Wholesaler to a late cafe: 'We put last month down to a busy season. From today we take silence as a no to our terms. PAY NOW — 2 minutes.'
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016
doubt: Includes a real cut-off threat; tested against no letter

opening: Assembly opened with a video of young people who had done the programme showing what they did
picture: short film of last year's participants in action
beat: standard presentation (26.1%); a past participant live on stage (23.3%)
result: 34.4% filled in an interest form vs 26.1% standard vs 23.3% speaker on stage (+32%)
measured_by: BIT randomised trial, N = 34,835
family: film of people like you doing it
why: The audience sees the activity; an amateur live speaker was no better than the usual talk.
for_client: Climbing gym at a school fair: 40-second film of last term's beginners on the wall instead of a coach's speech
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016

opening: One-page 'Pension Passport' instead of the thick wake-up pack
beat: standard pension wake-up pack
result: ten times more likely to visit the Pension Wise website
measured_by: BIT/LV= randomised trial; N not in the passage read
family: one page instead of a pack
why: One sheet can be read; the pack is put aside.
for_client: Home insurance renewal: one page 'Your house in six numbers' instead of the booklet
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2016-17, 2017
doubt: Base rate very low; N not read

opening: A flu shot is waiting for you at Walmart.
seller: Walmart Pharmacy — text message, 72 hours after 'It’s flu season & you can get a flu shot at Walmart'
beat: no message (29.4%); 21 other texts incl. jokes (+1.9 to 2.1), 'healthier, wealthier, more educated' (+1.1), 'think about risk at specific locations' (+0.9)
result: +2.9 points vs 29.4% control (+9.9%; 2.7 points after shrinkage); best of 22
measured_by: Randomised, preregistered, N = 689,693
family: it is waiting for you
why: It is spoken of as already his, and the second text repeats it.
for_client: Bakery: 'It's Thursday and the sourdough is out.' then on Saturday: 'Your Saturday loaf is waiting for you at the counter.'
source: Milkman et al., A 680,000-person megastudy of nudges to encourage vaccination in pharmacies, PNAS 2022

opening: Come back and get your flu shot (one text)
seller: Walmart Pharmacy — text message to last year's customers
beat: other single texts: jokes (+1.9-2.1), avoid getting sick (+1.5), think about risk (+1.4)
result: +2.5 points vs 29.4% control, the best of the single-text messages
measured_by: Randomised, N = 689,693 in all, at least 27,365 per arm
family: come back
why: It treats the reader as a returning customer and tells him the one act.
for_client: Barber: 'Come back and get your summer cut.'
source: Milkman et al., A 680,000-person megastudy of nudges to encourage vaccination in pharmacies, PNAS 2022
doubt: Exact text is in the supplement; the table prints the label

opening: this is a reminder that a flu vaccine has been reserved for your appointment
seller: Penn Medicine and Geisinger — text 24 h before the visit
beat: usual care (42%); 18 other texts, among the weakest a joke told by a dog to a cat
result: +4.6 points vs 42% (+11%; 2.8 points after correction); best of 19 in both health systems
measured_by: Randomised, preregistered, N = 47,306
family: reserved for you
why: Something is already set aside in his name; the plain official voice fits the sender.
for_client: Optician: 'A reminder that a free lens clean has been reserved for your fitting on Tuesday.'
source: Milkman et al., A megastudy of text-based nudges ... upcoming doctor's appointment, PNAS 2021
doubt: A 2022-23 trial at UCLA with the same sentence (262,085 patients) found no effect on the whole list, only a small one (aRR 1.04) among people with a booked visit

opening: Hand hygiene prevents patients from catching diseases.
picture: sign above the soap and gel dispenser
beat: Hand hygiene prevents you from catching diseases. / Gel in, wash out.
result: soap and gel used 37.25% -> 54.18% (over 45% more); 'you' sign and slogan no change; second test: hand washing 80.69% -> 89.20% vs 80.00% -> 79.71%
measured_by: Two randomised field experiments in one hospital: 66 dispensers; 8 units, 567 observed opportunities
family: it protects the one you serve
why: For people who serve others, the other person's harm moves more than their own.
for_client: To restaurant owners, non-slip floor: 'Dry floors keep your waitress from falling' instead of 'Protect yourself from claims'
source: Grant & Hofmann, It's Not All About Me, Psychological Science 2011
doubt: Two weeks only; readers were professionals

opening: JOIN YOUR FELLOW GUESTS IN HELPING TO SAVE THE ENVIRONMENT. Almost 75% of guests who are asked to participate in our new resource savings program do help by using their towels more than once.
picture: door-hanger sign on the bathroom towel rail
beat: HELP SAVE THE ENVIRONMENT. You can show your respect for nature and help save the environment by reusing your towels during your stay.
result: 44.1% vs 35.1% reused towels (+9 points, +26%)
measured_by: Randomised by room, 1,058 occasions, 433 analysed
family: join the 75% who do it here
why: People do what people in the same place do.
for_client: Cafe: 'JOIN OUR MORNING GUESTS. 3 in 4 now bring their own cup.' (true number only)
source: Goldstein, Cialdini, Griskevicius, A Room with a Viewpoint, Journal of Consumer Research 35, 2008
doubt: Replications in Germany (Bohner & Schlueter 2014, N = 724 and 204) found no advantage over the ordinary environment card

opening: In a study conducted in Fall 2003, 75% of the guests who stayed in this room (#313) participated in our new resource savings program by using their towels more than once.
picture: sign on the towel rail naming the room number
beat: HELP SAVE THE ENVIRONMENT (37.2%); other 75% norms: fellow guests 44.0%, citizens 43.5%, men and women 40.9%
result: 49.3% vs 37.2% standard (+12.1 points, +33%) vs 42.8% other norms
measured_by: Randomised by room, 1,595 occasions
family: people in exactly this place
why: The closer the place, the stronger the example.
for_client: Barbershop chair card: '7 of 10 people who sat in this chair last month booked their next cut before standing up.'
source: Goldstein, Cialdini, Griskevicius, A Room with a Viewpoint, Journal of Consumer Research 35, 2008
doubt: German replication found no consistent effect of proximity

opening: Please don’t remove the petrified wood from the park
picture: a visitor stealing a piece of wood, red circle-and-bar over his hand
seller: Petrified Forest National Park — path sign
beat: Please leave petrified wood in the park (5.33%); 'Many past visitors have removed the petrified wood ...' (7.92%)
result: 1.67% of marked pieces taken vs 5.33% (positive wording) vs 7.92% ('many visitors have removed')
measured_by: Field experiment, 2,655 visitors, 1,140 marked pieces, signs rotated
family: a clear don't with the act crossed out
why: A negative is noticed more; saying 'many do it' teaches people to do it.
for_client: Tile shop: 'Please don't seal new stone in the first 48 hours' with the brush crossed out, instead of 'Please let stone rest'
source: Cialdini et al., Managing social norms for persuasive impact, Social Influence 1(1), 2006

opening: (after handing out one chocolate each and starting to leave, the waitress turns back:) she offers each guest one more piece of his choice
picture: a basket of miniature chocolates, offered a second time after turning back
beat: two pieces offered at once; one piece; no candy
result: tip per bill rose with each step: no candy 18.95%, one piece 19.59%, two at once 21.62%, one then one more 22.99% (t = 2.06, p = .02); in the first study 17.8% vs 15.1% (no candy)
measured_by: Randomised by shuffled cards: 92 dining parties; 80 dining parties
family: the unexpected second gift, for you
why: The same amount given as a spontaneous extra feels personal, and people give back.
for_client: Flower shop: wraps the bouquet, turns away, turns back — 'take this rose too, for your table'
source: Strohmetz, Rind, Fisher, Lynn, Sweetening the Till, J. Applied Social Psychology 2002 (manuscript)
doubt: One waitress; small samples

opening: Please take a few minutes to complete this for us. Thank you!
picture: handwritten yellow Post-it at the upper right of the cover page
beat: the same words handwritten on the cover sheet (48%); no note (36%); blank Post-it 43%
result: 76% returned vs 48% vs 36%; second study 69% vs 43% blank note vs 34%
measured_by: Randomised: 150 professors (50 per arm); second study 105; later studies 100 and 180
family: handwritten note from a person
why: It is seen first and reads as one person's favour.
for_client: Landscaper's quote with a yellow handwritten note: 'Mrs Hill, look at the terrace sketch first. Thanks! Ben'
source: Garner, Post-It Note Persuasion: A Sticky Influence, J. Consumer Psychology 15(3), 2005
doubt: University staff and students; repeated by Irish Revenue with businesses (19.2% -> 36.0%)

opening: We are expecting you at [clinic] on [date] at [time]. Not attending costs NHS £160 approx. Call 02077673200 if you need to cancel or rearrange.
seller: Barts Health NHS Trust — appointment text
beat: Appt at [clinic] on [date] at [time]. To cancel or rearrange call the number on your appointment letter. (11.1%); '9 out of 10 people attend'; 'Please be fair to others waiting' (10.7%); 'Not attending wastes NHS money' (9.9%)
result: missed 8.4% vs 11.1% control (-24%); repeated: 8.2% vs 9.9% general cost, 10.7% empathy, 9.6% recording
measured_by: Two randomised trials: 10,111 and 9,848 appointments
family: we expect you, and the exact cost of not coming
why: An exact sum nobody knew; the same idea without the number did less.
for_client: Hair salon text: 'We are expecting you Friday 10.30. An empty chair costs our stylist about £45. Call 555 010 to move it.'
source: Hallsworth et al., Stating Appointment Costs in SMS Reminders Reduces Missed Hospital Appointments, PLoS ONE 2015

opening: Nine out of ten people in the UK pay their tax on time. You are currently in the very small minority of people who have not paid us yet.
seller: HM Revenue and Customs — late payers
beat: plain letter; 'Nine out of ten people pay their tax on time' (+1.3 points); 'Paying tax means we all gain from vital public services ...' (+1.6)
result: +5.1 percentage points paid within 23 days against the plain letter (3.8 without covariates); repeated the next year (+4.2 / +4.7)
measured_by: Two natural field experiments, about 101,000 and about 119,000 taxpayers (17,000 per letter in the first)
family: most do; you are one of the few
why: The norm alone is weak; pointing out that the reader is outside it makes it bite.
for_client: Allotment club: 'Nine of ten plots have paid for the new water line. Yours is one of the few left.'
source: Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe, Vlaev, The Behavioralist as Tax Collector, J. Public Economics 2017 (WRAP copy)

opening: The great majority of people in your local area pay their tax on time. Most people with a debt like yours have paid it by now.
seller: HM Revenue and Customs — late payers
beat: general norm (+1.4), local norm alone (+2.2), same-debt norm alone (+3.0), plain letter
result: +5.0 percentage points, a 14.8% relative rise
measured_by: Natural field experiment, 13 messages, second year
family: people near you and in your situation
why: Two likenesses add up: same place and same situation.
for_client: Roofer: 'Most homes on Mill Lane with a 1970s roof like yours have had it checked since the storm.'
source: Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe, Vlaev, The Behavioralist as Tax Collector, J. Public Economics 2017 (WRAP copy)

opening: $5 a day
seller: Acorns — automatic saving (recurring deposit) screen in the app
result: 29.9% signed up vs 10.3% vs 7.1% (about 4x); after three months 19% still in vs 5%
measured_by: Randomised field experiment, 1,772 / 1,826 / 1,744 new users
family: the small daily sum
why: Five dollars a day compares with small daily spending; the monthly sum compares with bills.
for_client: Music school: 'Lessons for €3 a day' instead of '€90 a month'
source: Hershfield, Shu, Benartzi, Temporal Reframing and Participation in a Savings Program, Marketing Science 2020 (SSRN copy)
doubt: Daily people dropped out more in month one (75% stayed vs 86%); in a charity mailing the monthly sum beat the daily one by 71%

opening: Sushila worked as a school teacher and retired comfortably. But she became destitute when her husband passed away and other family members refused to support her.
picture: photograph of Sushila, one named elderly woman
seller: HelpAge India — Support a Gran flyer
beat: routine appeal sheet (0.11%); the same story of four unnamed ladies with a collage; the story without its first sentence
result: 0.36% gave vs 0.11% control (3.3 times)
measured_by: Randomised field experiment, 184,396 mailings, about 14,000 per version
family: one named person who had what you have, and lost it
why: One face and name, and a fall from an ordinary life like the reader's.
for_client: Physiotherapist: 'Marek laid floors for 20 years. Then one morning he could not lift his own tool bag.'
source: Sudhir, Roy, Cherian, Do Sympathy Biases Induce Charitable Giving?, Cowles 1940 (Marketing Science 2016)
doubt: Best of 12 = named + in-group + past + monthly sum together; each part tested separately too

opening: Buy ten car washes, get one free — card handed over with two stamps already on it
picture: a loyalty card with the first two of ten squares already stamped
beat: card of eight squares, none stamped (the same eight washes to buy)
result: 34% redeemed vs 19% (+15 points, +79%); and bought 2.9 days sooner each time
measured_by: Randomised, 300 cards, nine months
family: you have already started
why: A task already begun is finished more often than one not begun.
for_client: Dog groomer: 'Your card of six washes — first two are on us' instead of a card of four empty squares
source: Nunes & Dreze, The Endowed Progress Effect, J. Consumer Research 2006

opening: Stanford Residents Are Changing: Now Most Use Full Loads! Help Stanford Conserve Water!
picture: sign in the laundry room
beat: Most Stanford Residents Use Full Loads! Help Stanford Conserve Water!
result: laundry loads fell by nearly 30% over three weeks vs just under 10% with the 'most' sign
measured_by: Field experiment, three high-rise buildings
family: people here are changing
why: A movement is joined; a habit of others is only noted.
for_client: Shop door: 'Mill Street is changing: most of us now bring our own bag' (if true)
source: Sparkman & Walton, Dynamic Norms Promote Sustainable Behavior, Psychological Science 2017
doubt: Three buildings only

opening: Specifically, recent research has shown that, over the last 5 years, 30% of Americans have started to make an effort to limit their meat consumption.
seller: University cafe — text read before ordering
beat: 30% of Americans make an effort to limit their meat consumption (17%); unrelated text
result: 34% ordered a meatless lunch vs 17% static norm (doubled)
measured_by: Field experiment in a cafe queue, 304 people
family: more and more people have started
why: A minority that is growing can be joined; a fixed minority cannot.
for_client: Bike shop: 'In the last five years one in four offices here has started paying for staff bikes.'
source: Sparkman & Walton, Dynamic Norms Promote Sustainable Behavior, Psychological Science 2017
doubt: Later and larger studies found small or no effect on meat orders (BIT EAST 2024: 'the jury remains out')

opening: UCLA Health: [participant’s first name], a COVID-19 vaccine has just been made available to you at UCLA Health. Claim your dose today by making a vaccination appointment here:
beat: no text; basic reminder without 'just been made available to you / claim your dose'
result: with this wording +6.83 points appointments (+94.84%) and +4.12 points vaccinated (+29.63%) against no text; best of the four reminders
measured_by: Randomised trial, 93,354 people (first reminder)
family: yours has just arrived, claim it
why: The thing already belongs to the reader; he only has to fetch it.
for_client: Frame shop: 'Lena, your summer print slot has just opened. Claim it here.'
source: Dai et al., Behavioural nudges increase COVID-19 vaccinations, Nature 2021
doubt: Part of the lift is the reminder itself

opening: A private donor who believes in the importance of the project has given this campaign a grant in the amount of $10,000 to cover all the overhead costs associated with raising the needed donations…
beat: plain letter (3.36%); seed money $10,000 (4.75%); matching grant $10,000, $1:$1 (4.41%)
measured_by: Randomised mailing, 40,000 people, 10,000 per letter
family: your whole money goes to the thing itself
why: Someone else already paid the part nobody wants to pay.
for_client: Furniture maker's sponsor day: 'Our supplier has paid all the workshop costs this week: every euro goes into your table's wood.' (only if true)
source: Gneezy, Keenan, Gneezy, Avoiding overhead aversion in charity, Science 2014

opening: Make one gift now and we'll never ask for another donation again.
picture: envelope with photographs of children with clefts and the headline
beat: Smile Train's own best control packages after years of testing
result: 0.66% vs 0.34% gave (+93% donors); $56 vs $50 gift; $152,928 vs $71,566 (+114%); later gifts equal ($107,855 vs $107,043); nearly 50% more in total
measured_by: Five mailing waves; 415,226 households got the line
family: we will never ask again
why: It is against the sender's interest and frees the reader; he gives back once for the kindness.
for_client: Newsletter of a garden centre: 'Tell us once what you grow. We will never ask again.' Car servicing: 'One call. We won't ring you again.'
source: Kamdar, Levitt, List, Mullaney, Syverson, Once and Done, working paper 2015

opening: Letter naming the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation as the giver who doubles the reader's gift ($2 for each $1)
beat: the same match from an unnamed donor (experiment 2); no match (experiment 1)
result: naming the giver: +51% money per letter; against no match: +81% money and +79% donors
measured_by: Two randomised mailings (prior donors; cold lists)
family: a name you trust has already put its own money in
why: The careful giver's money says the thing is good.
for_client: New baby food: 'The city's children's hospital already buys it for its wards' — the named buyer first (true only)
source: Karlan & List, How Can Bill and Melinda Gates Increase Other People's Donations, 2012
doubt: The letter's own words are not printed in the passage read; N in the paper's tables

opening: We had another member, they contributed $300. How much would you like to pledge today?
beat: no mention; $75; $180
result: average $119.70 vs about $106.72 (+12%); first-time givers +29% ($25.33)
measured_by: Field experiment, 538 callers; the named gifts were real
family: what another person just did
why: A real, fairly high example sets what is normal for a newcomer.
for_client: Caterer on the phone: 'The last school we did took the 40-person table. How many are you?' (real case)
source: Shang & Croson, A Field Experiment in Charitable Contribution, 2006 version (Economic Journal 2009)
doubt: No effect on renewing members; $75 and $180 not significant; a low example can lower gifts (Costa Rica park)

opening: A table plaque with the five most popular dishes, by number of dishes sold in the previous week
picture: small plaque on the table listing five dish names
seller: Mei Zhou Dong Po — Sichuan restaurant chain, Beijing
beat: no plaque; a plaque with five 'sample dishes' (names only)
result: demand for the five dishes +13 to 18%; a plaque that only names dishes: no significant effect
measured_by: Randomised field experiment, 13 sites, tables randomised
family: most ordered last week
why: Others' real choices are information; mere mention is not.
for_client: Hardware shop shelf card: 'Five most bought here last week' with the five items
source: Cai, Chen, Fang, Observational Learning, NBER 13516 (AER 2009)

opening: Hello, I am a professor at Harvard studying the opinions, decision-making, goals, and expectations of school board members. I would like to learn from you how school district leaders are thinking about the challenges facing schools right now. Would you please complete this brief survey?
seller: Harvard researcher — survey request to school board members
beat: the same e-mail with the flattery and reasons left in (127 words)
result: 4.8% answered vs 2.7% (+78%); 49 words vs 127
measured_by: Randomised, 7,002 school board members
family: who I am, what I want, done
why: Readers judge by length how much work the request is.
for_client: Event caterer to schools: 'Hello, I cook for school fairs in Leeds. Could you tell me your date? It takes one line.'
source: Rogers & Lasky-Fink, When Writing for Busy Readers, Less Is More, Behavioral Scientist, 2023

opening: Thank you for participating in [district name] summer updates! / (second text) Please answer this 1-minute survey to help us improve our program [survey link].
seller: EveryDay Labs for school districts — text message
beat: the same two sentences in a single text
result: +15% answered
measured_by: Randomised, 22,694 parents
family: the ask stands alone
why: The request is seen without hunting for it.
for_client: Garage: text 1 'Thanks for bringing the van in today!' text 2 'One question: was it ready when we said? [link]'
source: Rogers & Lasky-Fink, Write shorter messages, The Boston Globe, 2020

opening: Cumberland-Spiced Veggie Sausage & Mash
beat: Meat-Free Sausage and Mash
result: sales +76%
measured_by: Sainsbury's / WRI Better Buying Lab, August-October 2017; N not given
family: place and taste instead of what is missing
why: It names where the taste comes from; the old name named an absence.
for_client: Sugar-free bakery: 'Sicilian Almond Biscuit' instead of 'Sugar-free biscuit'
source: World Resources Institute (Better Buying Lab), It's All in a Name: How to Boost the Sales of Plant-Based Menu Items, 2019

opening: Cuban Black Bean Soup
seller: Panera Bread — menu name, 18 Los Angeles cafes
beat: Low Fat Vegetarian Black Bean Soup
result: sales +13%
measured_by: Month-long naming test, January 2018; N not given
family: place and taste instead of what is missing
why: The origin promises flavour; 'low fat' promises none.
for_client: Massage studio: 'Forest-pine back massage' instead of 'Hypoallergenic massage'
source: World Resources Institute (Better Buying Lab), It's All in a Name: How to Boost the Sales of Plant-Based Menu Items, 2019

opening: Field Grown Breakfast
beat: Meat-free Breakfast (and Garden Breakfast +12%)
result: sales +17%
measured_by: Sainsbury's / WRI Better Buying Lab; N not given
family: where it grew
why: The eater sees the field; the old name saw no meat.
for_client: Juice bar: 'Orchard Press' instead of 'No-added-sugar juice'
source: World Resources Institute (Better Buying Lab), It's All in a Name: How to Boost the Sales of Plant-Based Menu Items, 2019

opening: Garden Breakfast
beat: Meat-free Breakfast
result: sales +12%
measured_by: Sainsbury's / WRI Better Buying Lab; N not given
family: where it grew
why: Warm place word instead of a lack.
for_client: Florist-cafe: 'Greenhouse lunch' instead of 'vegan lunch'
source: World Resources Institute (Better Buying Lab), It's All in a Name: How to Boost the Sales of Plant-Based Menu Items, 2019

opening: Rich Buttery Roasted Sweet Corn / Zesty Ginger Turmeric Sweet Potatoes
beat: healthy-restrictive labels; basic labels, for the identical dish
result: chosen 41% more often than under 'healthy restrictive' names, 25% more than under plain names
measured_by: Turnwald, Boles, Crum, JAMA Internal Medicine 2017, as reported by WRI; N not given there
family: say the taste, not the virtue
why: People choose by expected pleasure.
for_client: Toothpaste for children: 'Crushed strawberry foam' instead of 'Fluoride cavity protection'
source: World Resources Institute (Better Buying Lab), It's All in a Name: How to Boost the Sales of Plant-Based Menu Items, 2019

opening: Herb n’ Honey Balsamic Glazed Turnips
seller: US university dining halls — dish label
beat: Healthy Choice Turnips; Turnips
result: taste labels: +29% chosen against health labels, +14% against plain; +39% eaten by weight against health labels
measured_by: Preregistered multi-site trial, 5 universities, 137,842 diner decisions, 185 days, 24 vegetables
family: say the taste, not the virtue
why: Expected pleasure; works best where the food really tastes good.
for_client: Bakery: 'Toasted walnut and date rye' instead of 'High-fibre rye'
source: Turnwald et al., Increasing Vegetable Intake by Emphasizing Tasty and Enjoyable Attributes, Psychological Science 2019

opening: Sizzlin’ Szechuan Green Beans with Toasted Garlic
seller: US university dining halls — dish label
beat: Nutritious Green Beans; Green Beans
result: see pooled result: +29% against health labels, +14% against plain
measured_by: 5 universities, 137,842 diner decisions
family: say the taste, not the virtue
why: Sound, place and roasted flavour in six words.
for_client: Candle maker: 'Crackling cedar and burnt orange' instead of 'Natural soy candle'
source: Turnwald et al., Increasing Vegetable Intake by Emphasizing Tasty and Enjoyable Attributes, Psychological Science 2019

opening: Twisted Citrus Glazed Carrots
seller: US university dining halls — dish label

opening: Did you know that working off a bottle of soda or fruit juice takes about 5 miles of walking?

beat: hiding the trouble, as the dealers wanted
result: People flocked by the thousands to buy, and the store was saved
measured_by: told by Hopkins; 'thousands', no count
family: blunt confession of the true reason for the sale
why: Truth was such a rarity in advertising that the announcement made a sensation.
for_client: A furniture shop losing its lease (true): 'Our landlord wants us out by 30 June. We have 41 sofas and nowhere to put them.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "How I Got My Start in Advertising"
doubt: Hopkins writes 'read something like this'; second-hand anecdote, no count.

opening: We have 1,200 rotten mackintoshes. They are almost worthless, but still worth the price we ask. Come and see them.
seller: a store's mackintoshes (copy: John E. Powers)
beat: the mackintoshes could not be disposed of before
result: every mackintosh sold (1,200) before the buyer calmed down
measured_by: told by Hopkins; 1,200 coats
family: damning your own goods, then the price
why: The seller says the fault first, so the price is believed.
for_client: A tile shop: 'We have 300 boxes of ugly brown tiles. They are still worth 4 euros. Come and look.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "How I Got My Start in Advertising"
doubt: Second-hand anecdote about John Powers; a collector's tale repeated in many books.

opening: [half-page newspaper ads announcing the biggest cake in the world]
picture: a cake baked with Cotosuet, decorated and built as high as the room, in the bay window of a new store
beat: six weeks of ordinary advertising, in which sales 'hardly increased at all'
result: during the next week 105,000 people climbed four flights of stairs to that cake; Cotosuet was placed on a profit-paying basis in Chicago
measured_by: Hopkins; visitors counted 105,000 in one week; sales figure not given
family: the world's biggest (spectacle that proves the product)
why: No argument in the world can ever compare with one dramatic demonstration; every guesser of the weight had to buy a pail.
for_client: A mattress shop: 'The biggest bed in the city stands in our window on Saturday. Forty children will jump on it.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Larger Fields"
doubt: Own account. A weight-guessing contest requiring a purchase was attached (a prize draw on purchase: do not copy that part). Exact printed words are not given in the book; the bracket describes the opening.

opening: Evening News. All about the Big Cake.
picture: newsboys on Main Street crying papers
result: stores mobbed in every city; profit insured in advance by carload orders; thousands of regular users in every city
measured_by: Hopkins; no counts beyond carload orders
family: news cry about a spectacle
why: The spectacle was told as news, not as an advertisement.
for_client: A bakery's local story: 'News from Mill Street: the 2-metre loaf goes in the oven at 6.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Larger Fields"
doubt: Own account; no figures for this leg.

opening: I have come from Chicago to consult you about a card.
picture: a coloured street-car card of the ideal pie, put fifty feet away so that the baker looks at it
beat: six salesmen of the Boston branch asking bakers to buy at half a cent a pound over the rival
result: more orders for Cotosuet (one man, about a week) than six salesmen had sold in six weeks; not one buyer complained about the price
measured_by: Swift's order books as told by Hopkins; N bakers not given; no leading baker refused
family: ask the buyer's expert judgment first
why: He was a pie expert and I wanted his ideas; nobody had asked him to be an adviser before; the sale was the buyer's own advertising.
for_client: A web studio to a restaurant owner: 'I have come to ask your opinion on one photograph of a lamb dish.' Then: 'Would you like it as your front page?'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Personal Salesmanship"
doubt: Own account; the seller (advertising manager) had a card and prestige the salesmen did not.

opening: Try this cough remedy; watch the benefits it brings. It cannot harm, for no opiates are in it. If it succeeds, the cough will stop. If it fails, it is free. Your own druggist signs the warrant.
seller: Dr. Shoop — cough cure, sold through druggists
beat: rivals' claims and testimonials; guarantees signed by makers a thousand miles away
result: enormous results on the cough cure; 'it worked like magic' on the others; spending grew to $400,000 per year in newspaper advertising, at one-third of the former cost of results
measured_by: Hopkins, sales through druggists; spend $400,000 a year; no split given
family: guarantee signed by a person you know
why: People bought results, and the guarantor was the neighbour to whom they paid their money, not a stranger.
for_client: A dentist's whitening page: 'If your shade has not changed by two in 14 days, your own hygienist, Mrs Okafor, signs the refund at the desk.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Medical Advertising"
doubt: Patent medicine: Hopkins himself says he no longer approves. Guarantee covered six bottles for five dollars; few users bought that many. 'Said in effect' — wording not verbatim ad. The refund tied to six bottles gave confidence to one-bottle buyers who were not covered by it: copy only a guarantee that covers the purchase advertised.

opening: [sixteen hours required to bake beans at home; crisped beans on top, mushy beans below — exact headline not printed]
picture: home-baked beans, crisped on top and mushy below, beside whole mealy factory beans
seller: Van Camp Packing Company — pork and beans
beat: all advertisers of pork and beans crying 'Buy my brand'; copy already tried from New York and Philadelphia was refused
result: an enormous success; an enormous demand; a much higher price than rivals
measured_by: Hopkins; sales not given; a field survey found 94 per cent of housewives baked at home, 6 per cent reachable by brand copy
family: attack the old way of doing it, not the rival brand
why: Investigators found 94 per cent of housewives baked their own, so the enemy was home baking and not another can.
for_client: A catering firm: 'Your party takes eleven hours in your own kitchen. Here is where the hours go.' with the photo of the burnt and the raw tray.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "The Start of My Seventeen Years"
doubt: Own account; result stated only in words ('enormous success'). Scientific Advertising gives the canvass as 4 / 96 percent of some thousands of homes, My Life 6 / 94. Immigrant Entrepreneurship (Lasker entry) confirms the campaign against home baking (too hard, too mushy, slow) but gives no sales figure and credits Lasker's house. Exact printed words are not given in the book; the bracket describes the opening.

opening: [ad announcing the number of restaurants and lunch counters serving Van Camp's at noon and how many men went somewhere for it every day]
seller: Van Camp Packing Company — pork and beans
beat: earlier copy
result: soon thousands of places serving; 'that set women thinking' and housewives were ready to quit baking; enormous demand
measured_by: Hopkins; number of places announced but not printed in the book
family: how many people already choose it, and where
why: The trend of the crowd: wives learned their own men folk were buying it downtown.
for_client: A lunch-box service: '312 people in the Harbour Street offices ate our lentil soup on Tuesday. Your husband may be one.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "The Start of My Seventeen Years"
doubt: Part of one campaign, result not separated; exact words not printed.

opening: [full-page Sunday ad with a coupon good at any store for a ten-cent can of Van Camp's evaporated milk, announced three weeks ahead]
seller: Van Camp Packing Company — evaporated milk
beat: house-to-house free samples, which leave stores unstocked and cheapen the product; a rival brand dominated New York
result: 1,460,000 coupons presented in Greater New York; $146,000 redeemed; total cost $175,000; came back with profit in less than nine months; 97 per cent distribution in three weeks
measured_by: Hopkins; coupons redeemed, several medium cities first as a test, then Greater New York
family: announced free full-size product at your own shop
why: The woman had to read the story and make an effort, and every grocer saw a ten-cent sale he would lose.
for_client: A new soap brand: three weeks of 'On Sunday 14 June this page pays for your first bar at Boots' and then the page.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "The Start of My Seventeen Years"
doubt: Own account; the 1,460,000 count was vast for Greater New York homes; not checked by others. No independent confirmation found. 1,460,000 'homes' looks larger than the number of families in New York then [mine, UNVERIFIED]; multiple papers per home are likely. Scientific Advertising calls them 'requests' and advises NOT to announce the date (papers get bought up), My Life says it was announced for three weeks. Exact printed words are not given in the book; the bracket describes the opening.

opening: [a secret gift: wrapped presents in the grocer's window, nobody told what they were, one for six Van Camp labels]
picture: piled wrapped presents in the grocers' windows
seller: Van Camp Packing Company — evaporated milk
beat: describing the gift ('some will decide that they want it, more will decide that they don't'); the earlier coupon plan, copied by rivals
result: countless women bought six cans; 'We captured and held many a big market in that way'; the gift cost more than the profit on the sale
measured_by: Hopkins; no counts
family: secret gift (curiosity)
why: Describe a gift and some want it and more do not; everybody wants a secret gift.
for_client: A soap maker: 'One wrapped box on the counter. Bring six wrappers and take it. We will not say what is in it.' (worth more than they expect)
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "The Start of My Seventeen Years"
doubt: No counts; the gift must be better than expected or the trick turns on the seller.

opening: [chief engineer Howard E. Coffin named and shown as the maker of the car; later 48 named and pictured engineers of the Hudson]
picture: the engineer's face and name; for Hudson, a board of forty-eight engineers
seller: Chalmers, then Hudson Motor Car Company
beat: an older, handsomer rival at the same price (Cadillac) sold by its name
result: gave the Chalmers a distinction which brought it great success; the Hudson was a great success and Hopkins ran its advertising for seven years
measured_by: Hopkins; sales not given
family: a named person behind the product
why: People like to deal with men whose names are connected with certain accomplishments, rather than soulless corporations.
for_client: A roofing company: 'Roofs by Ines Duarte, 22 years on ladders. Her number is on every roof.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Automobile Advertising"
doubt: Own account; no figures. Today's history adds that Chalmers/Hudson were also good-value cars. Exact printed words are not given in the book; the bracket describes the opening.

opening: The Wonderful Overland Story
year: 1908-1910 (first advertising they ever did; year not given)
beat: a list of the car's features ('nothing in all the data I gathered appealed to me like the romance')
result: The Overland became, as it is today, one of the largest-selling cars in the world; no figures
measured_by: Hopkins; see doubt
family: the story of how demand forced the maker to grow
why: People go with the crowd: it told how users' demand kept outgrowing the factory until cars were built in tents.
for_client: A noodle shop: 'The Wonderful Story of Table 9' — how the queue outgrew the shop three times.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Automobile Advertising"
doubt: Story told from memory and not vouched for by him; result in words only; the car sold well by word of mouth before the ads.

opening: John W. Bate, Efficiency Expert
beat: other car advertising of the time
result: I never knew any automobile advertising to bring so many inquiries; sales started at an amazing rate; the company was recapitalized in a large way
measured_by: Hopkins; inquiries and sales, no figures
family: named expert on what men are already talking about
why: Efficiency was then a popular subject with men in all lines; the headline named the man and told his methods.
for_client: A roofing firm in an energy crisis: 'Sana Iqbal, Heat-Loss Expert, walked your roof.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Automobile Advertising"
doubt: The car was bad (hundreds came back) and the company was destroyed by it: the opening won inquiries and sales but ruined the brand.

opening: No-Rim-Cut Tires, 10% Oversize
beat: the manufacturer's own talk of the 'straight-side' tire, which Hopkins himself had never bothered to understand
result: immediate and enormous; sales grew by leaps and bounds; Goodyear soon occupied the leading place; advertising grew from $40,000 to nearly $2,000,000 per year
measured_by: Hopkins / Goodyear spending and sales rank; sales not given
family: result in the name, plus a number
why: Results are what men are after; they care not how you get them — the name says the result, the figure makes it exact.
for_client: A window firm: 'No-Draft Windows, 10% More Light' instead of 'triple chamber profile'.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Tire Advertising"
doubt: Own account; advertising spend also rose 50-fold (30,000 named dealers in the papers as well), so the headline's share is not isolated. Goodyear's own ad of 5 Jan 1913 states 918,687 tires sold in 1912 and demand 12 times larger than three years before, which supports the growth; Archivio Copy notes the dealer figures have no independent confirmation and authorship of single ads is disputed. CBC Radio gives the lead to the All-Weather tread name.

opening: Note how many new cars now have Goodyear tires.
picture: heading 'No-Rim-Cut Tires, 10% Oversize, On the Latest Cars'
beat: No-Rim-Cut claim, which rivals had copied within two or three years
result: the ad itself states: 918,687 tires sold last year, demand 12 times larger than three years ago, nearly half of all new cars; Hopkins: kept Goodyear in the lead, advertising grew from $40,000 to nearly $2,000,000 a year
measured_by: Goodyear's own printed figures; Hopkins for the spend; no control
family: the crowd is turning to us
why: People follow the crowds, because it is hard for them to analyse reasons and worth.
for_client: A gym: photo of 41 empty bikes from 2019 and 41 full ones today, with the count in between.
source: Goodyear advertisement, Oregon newspaper (Historic Oregon Newspapers, sn85042444), 5 Jan 1913, seq 41; and Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, ch. 'Tire Advertising'
doubt: Figures are the company's own claim in its ad; they show the growth, not that this ad caused it. Found by the lead 'crowd' idea that Hopkins tells.

opening: [exact figures of mileage comparisons of bus lines on Miller tires, and the trend to Millers in commercial use]
picture: great machines wearing out all sorts of tires; buses
beat: the belief that good tires are about alike
result: a short but successful campaign; no figures
measured_by: Hopkins; no figures
family: the professionals' choice in exact numbers
why: Ordinary buyers cannot compare, but they know large users do not choose on guess.
for_client: A paint maker: 'Painters who buy by the pallet used 8,412 litres of ours last year.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Tire Advertising"
doubt: No figures; exact words not printed; a dispute with dealers ended it.

opening: We Will Buy
picture: a box above the ad: in a few days we will buy a cake of Palmolive for every woman who applies
seller: B. J. Johnson Soap Co. — Palmolive soap
beat: '10-Cent Cake Free' ('ro-Cent Cake Free' in the scan) and free samples on the doorstep
result: Benton Harbor test cost $700, repeat sales paid for the advertising before the bills were due; about $50,000 spent in tests of numerous cities, always with like results; advance dealer orders exceeded $100,000; Palmolive became the leading toilet soap of the world
measured_by: Hopkins; repeat sales in the test town, then many cities; figures 'may not be exact', from memory
family: we buy it for you (an owner's gesture, not a free sample)
why: When you offer to buy something for a woman, she wants to learn about it; 'free' cheapens the product, buying shows confidence.
for_client: A coffee roaster's ad: 'We Will Buy your first bag. Show this page at any grocer before Sunday.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Early History of Palmolive"
doubt: He states 'much better' without printing the comparative numbers; figures from memory; sample and beauty story changed along with the headline. Independent history of Palmolive checked below in the web rows. Independent check: Cosmetics and Skin confirms disappointing sales until an extensive campaign, name change of company in 1917; CBC Radio says best-selling soap in the world by 1916 and 99 per cent of drugstores stocked; a second-hand Lord & Thomas account (21st Night blog) gives Cleveland: coupons $2,000, ads $1,000, yearly sales $3,000 to $20,000. Soap dates from 1898-99.

opening: [the beauty appeal: Cleopatra and Roman beauties used palm and olive oils — exact first headline not printed in this book]
seller: B. J. Johnson Soap Co. — Palmolive soap
beat: nothing: the soap had slight distribution and was not considered an advertising possibility
result: the repeat sales in Benton Harbor paid for the advertising before the bills were due; same test ads in numerous other cities, always with like results; 'now the sales run to many millions yearly'
measured_by: Hopkins; sales, no exact figures
family: ancient beauty custom behind a present product
why: Simple things striking a popular chord; there is no stronger appeal to women than beauty.
for_client: A bath-house: 'The queens of the desert poured this oil on their hair. It is on our shelf.' (true ingredient only)
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Early History of Palmolive"
doubt: Credited to a group session; the first ad's headline is not given; no figure of this appeal alone.

opening: Foods shot from guns
picture: grains drawn at eight times normal size, shot from guns
seller: The Quaker Oats Company — Puffed Wheat and Puffed Rice
beat: being advertised for years as one of countless cereal foods with declining sales; a leading advertiser called the phrase the work of an imbecile
result: the most successful campaign ever conducted on cereals; made Puffed Wheat and Puffed Rice the largest money-earners in the field of breakfast foods, at prices raised to 15 and 10 cents
measured_by: Hopkins; sales history of the products, figures not given here
family: strange true process (curiosity)
why: It aroused curiosity, one of the greatest incentives; no one could read a puffed grain ad without wishing to see those grains.
for_client: A toast maker: 'Bread that is dropped from a tower' (only if that is really how it is done).
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Puffed Grains and Quaker Oats"
doubt: Own account, no sales figures; price, name, samples and magazines changed too. Independent check in the web rows. Scientific Advertising adds: 'These foods were failures before that factor was discovered' and the two other lines 'Grains puffed to 8 times the normal size', '125 million steam explosions caused in every kernel'. Independent check: F. L. Johnson, Minnesota History (2004) credits the first 'nationwide sensation' and nearly half a million dollars of added 1909 profit to ads on Prof. Anderson as a scientist and the 'Eighth Wonder of the World', and the new name Puffed Wheat, so the guns line was not alone and not the first. CBC Radio (retold from Lasker biographies) says the line sent sales up 300 per cent, 1913 - no primary source given.

opening: [calories in Quaker Oats shown conspicuously: cost per 1,000 calories about one-tenth the cost of meat]
seller: The Quaker Oats Company — Quaker Oats
beat: earlier Quaker Oats advertising
result: We doubled the Quaker Oats sales on that calorie presentation
measured_by: Hopkins/Quaker sales; doubled; no figures
family: a fad number turned into a price comparison
why: Calories were the fad; the number showed the saving against meat.
for_client: A lentil stew shop: '1,000 calories for 1.10 euro. The same in steak: 9 euro.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Puffed Grains and Quaker Oats"
doubt: Wartime meat shortage drove demand too; exact words not printed.

opening: [Pepsodent: beautiful teeth and the cloudy film on teeth, never disasters, shown with attractive people; free sample, not the price]
picture: attractive people with beautiful teeth
year: c. 1915-1916 launch; 52 countries and 17 languages by 1927
beat: prevention and penalty copy ('Scores have tried to scare people into using a certain tooth paste'); competitors
result: first test city: $1,000 came back with a profit before the bills were due; nation-wide demand in one year; worldwide in four years; sold in 52 countries, 17 languages; Hopkins made a million dollars on it
measured_by: Hopkins; keyed coupons on every ad, hundreds of ads, one test city then others
family: name the visible enemy (film), promise beauty
why: People do anything to cure a trouble, little to prevent it, and beauty was the chief appeal found by coupon.
for_client: A window cleaner: 'Run a finger over the glass: that film is your light going.' then a picture of a bright kitchen.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Pepsodent"
doubt: Own account of his own fortune; exact winning headlines are in Scientific Advertising, not here. Historians' checks are in the web rows. Independent check (Made-in-Chicago Museum): company sales $200,000 in the first year, $6 million in 1922, No. 1 within 18 months of the first national ad - supports the sales. But: the first 1917 ads were headed 'That Film on Teeth: The Source of All Tooth Troubles' and laid out like medical-journal papers (so Hopkins's 'I never referred to disasters' is not the whole story), and Franke & Gies (Journal of Dental Research 1919; Michigan Dental Journal 1917) found that the paste did not remove the film: the claim misled. Take the shape only for a true, visible film. Lasker, Smith and inventor Ruthrauff shared the authorship.

opening: The whole profit in our business is made by the customers who stay with us year after year... So I wish to offer you a token in appreciation of the fact that you continue with us.
seller: a thirty-year-old mail-order seller of garments
beat: same letter for everyone
result: part of the same scheme; sales per catalogue enormously increased
measured_by: Hopkins; no figures
family: different letter to old and new customers
why: The old customer hears that staying is worth something and is thanked.
for_client: A gym: 'You have been a member 400 days. That is what keeps the lights on.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Some Mail-Order Experiences"
doubt: No figures; result not split between the two letters.

opening: Let us help you for a week without cost or obligation
seller: maker of an electric sewing machine motor
beat: soliciting a purchase, which had been difficult
result: about nine in ten of the trials led to sales
measured_by: told by Hopkins; N of trials not given
family: help first for a week, a person comes with it
why: The offer was resistless: a motor for one week with a man to show how, no purchase asked.
for_client: A physiotherapy clinic: 'Let us help your back for a week without cost or obligation.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "3 Offer Service"
doubt: No control; those who asked for the trial were already interested.

opening: I was sent here to give you a brush. I have samples here and I want you to take your choice.
picture: a canvasser with samples at the door
beat: asking the housewives to buy
result: enormously successful in a line which would seem very difficult; some 2,000 canvassers
measured_by: told by Hopkins; sales not given
family: gift to choose from first
why: The housewife is all smiles, sees brushes she wants while picking, and wants to reciprocate the gift.
for_client: A soap maker at a market: 'I was sent to give you one bar. Pick the one you like.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "3 Offer Service"
doubt: No figure beyond 2,000 canvassers; told second-hand.

opening: Accept this package and try it. I'll come back in a few days to ask how you like it.
picture: half a pound of coffee handed over at the door
seller: a concern selling coffee and more by wagon
beat: asking for an order
result: run in some 500 cities; always some service
measured_by: told by Hopkins; figures not given beyond 500 cities
family: gift, then a question of taste
why: He never asks for an order; he asks an opinion and earns a utensil credit.
for_client: A tea seller: 'Take this tin and make a pot. I will come on Thursday to ask what you think.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "3 Offer Service"
doubt: No result number other than reach.

opening: [a $1,000 hat, advertised at one Easter time by a department store]
picture: the hat with its price
result: the floor could not hold the women who came to see it
measured_by: told by Hopkins; not counted; no sales of the hat given
family: shocking price as a spectacle
why: People judge largely by price; they come to see what costs so much.
for_client: A furniture shop: 'The 9,000-euro chair is in the window until Saturday. Sit on it.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: Crowd, not sales; undated; store not named. Exact printed words are not given in the book; the bracket describes the opening.

opening: Your name in gilt lettering on each book
beat: the same ads without the name (unprofitable)
result: with scarcely another change in the ads they sold some hundreds of thousands of books
measured_by: the advertiser: unprofitable before, hundreds of thousands sold after; no control group
family: your name on the thing
why: That name in gilt gave much added value to the books.
for_client: A diary maker: 'Your surname on the spine, in gold.' as the first line.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: Before/after, not a split. Same case as in My Life in Advertising (no figure there).

opening: [letter: a leather-covered book with your name on it is waiting for you and will be sent on request]
beat: sending small gifts (memorandum books) unasked: very small results
result: nearly all men filled out the request and supplied the information
measured_by: told by Hopkins; 'nearly all'; N not given
family: something of yours is waiting
why: When something has his name on it a man will make the effort to get it, even a trifle.
for_client: An accountant to shop owners: 'The folder with your company name on it is ready. Where shall I send it?'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: Told in general; no N; in My Life a life insurer is named. My Life in Advertising tells the same device for a life insurance company ('a reply from a very large percentage').

opening: Try our rivals too
seller: Van Camp Packing Company — pork and beans (named in My Life in Advertising)
beat: 'Look out for substitutes', 'Be sure you get this brand', with no effect
result: that corrected the situation; buyers were careful to get the brand
measured_by: told by Hopkins; not counted
family: invite comparison with the competitor
why: The maker could court a trial of the rest, so the product was conspicuously superior.
for_client: A shoe repairer: 'Take your old pair to two others first.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: No figures; the 'superior' claim is the writer's word. Also told in My Life in Advertising ('That appeal won over others'), where Hopkins admits nobody at the factory could pick Van Camp's blind: so 'superior' was not true of the taste.

opening: [coupon: the maker buys the package for you at retail price, at any store]
seller: maker of a food product (one of two nearly identical)
beat: the rival that gave the same full-size package free
result: the first (free) advertiser failed and even lost a large part of his trade; the second succeeded
measured_by: two advertisers with nearly identical goods, real market; not a split; no figures
family: we buy it for you, not free
why: It is hard to pay for an article which has once been free; an article good enough for the maker to buy is good enough to buy.
for_client: A noodle brand: 'We bought your first bowl at the corner shop. Show this.' instead of 'Free bowl'.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: Two firms differ in more than the offer; not named. The same phrase contradicts Hopkins's own point that 'Free' multiplies readers (see the rule on it). Exact printed words are not given in the book; the bracket describes the opening.

opening: Our net profit is 3 percent
seller: a mail-order seller of women's clothing
beat: 'Lowest prices in America' and a guarantee to undersell any dealer, both copied by rivals
result: the next year their business made a sensational increase
measured_by: the advertiser's sales, year after year; no figure
family: exact small profit instead of 'lowest price'
why: No one could be expected to do business on less than 3 percent, so their prices must be minimum.
for_client: An optician: 'Our profit on a pair is 11 pounds. Receipt attached.'
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "7 Being Specific"
doubt: Same case as in My Life; no figures; the firm also sold to low-income customers on credit (only the profit line is taken here). My Life adds: their books showed under 3 percent for years, so the figure was true.

opening: Our profit is 9 percent
picture: actual costs of the hidden parts of a $1,500 car, total $735
seller: Chalmers Motor Company — $1,500 car (named in My Life in Advertising)
beat: the general impression that profits were excessive
result: made a great success along those lines
measured_by: told by Hopkins; not counted
family: open the books
why: Actual figures are not generally discounted.
for_client: A tiler: 'The hidden 735 in your 1,500 bathroom' with a list.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "7 Being Specific"
doubt: No sales figures.

opening: Multiplies itself in lather 250 times
seller: Palmolive Shaving Cream (named in My Life in Advertising)
